awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  Steadi-scores: Translating Balance Science into Clinical Action for Proactive Balance Training
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this SBIR Phase I project is to improve balance health across the population through the development of an innovative and accessible solution for balance training and assessment. Balance declines naturally with age, often beginning around 40, and can go unnoticed until a fall highlights the issue. Falls frequently result in significant physical, emotional, and social challenges, underscoring the need for proactive tools to address balance health. This project aims to design a portable and affordable platform that individuals of all ages could use at home or in clinics to practice and improve their balance. The platform would offer engaging exercises while providing insights on balance progress that could help individuals better understand their balance health and take steps to mitigate fall risks. This innovation has the potential to fill a critical gap in the market by offering an accessible, cost-effective, and scalable approach to balance health. It could enhance scientific and technological understanding by leveraging new methods to measure and support balance. By addressing a widespread issue, this platform could meet a large market need in home and clinic-based healthcare, establishing a foundation for future commercial success while advancing health, mobility, and independence for a diverse population.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project addresses the challenge of integrating biomechanical balance metrics, such as center-of-pressure and sway data, with functional clinical assessments like the Mini-BESTest, which are commonly used to evaluate balance capabilities. Clinical assessments often rely on subjective ratings that can introduce bias and may fail to capture subtle improvements in individuals with higher balance abilities. On the other hand, biomechanical metrics provide objective, quantitative measures but lack a direct, clinically validated connection to functional outcomes. This project seeks to bridge this gap by investigating how biomechanical data from interactive balance activities can be aligned with clinically relevant measures. Using advanced machine learning techniques, the project will develop models to map biomechanical metrics to outcomes derived from the Mini-BESTest framework. These models will enable the creation of a clinically grounded balance score that reflects patient progress with greater specificity and sensitivity. The anticipated results include a robust framework for integrating biomechanical and clinical approaches, advancing balance assessment methodologies, and enhancing the accuracy of balance evaluations through data-driven tools. This work could provide clinicians with a scientifically validated method for tracking balance improvement and guiding interventions with greater precision.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Background: Good balance is a skill most people take for granted until it begins to fade. Yet the gradual loss of balance that comes with aging, injury, or illness is a leading cause of falls, resulting in 3 million emergency department visits, lost independence, and health care costs exceeding $80 billion in the United States annually. Detecting and addressing balance issues early is needed to lessen this growing problem.

Part of the problem is measurement. Instrumented balance assessment tools can be prohibitively expensive and difficult to translate into everyday clinical settings. The routine assessments clinicians typically use to measure balance can be time-consuming, cumbersome, require specialized training, and miss early or subtle changes, especially in people who still appear steady on their feet. As a result, many balance problems go undetected until after a fall has already happened.

Work Accomplished: This NSF-funded project tested whether a portable, game-based technology called Steadiplay could measure balance accurately enough to distinguish people at higher or lower risk of falling. Steadiplay uses a simple balance board that communicates wirelessly with a small tabletop robot, guiding users through short, engaging movement challenges. As a person plays, sensors on the board quietly record how their body sways and responds, turning a brief game into precise measurements of steadiness, reaction, and movement control.

To learn how well this works, the project enrolled 75 adults across a wide range of ages and balance abilities. Each person completed both the Steadiplay activities and a well-established clinical balance exam used by physical therapists. The central question was whether the Steadiplay measurements could reproduce the conclusions of that clinical exam.

The results were strong. Steadiplay correctly sorted people into higher and lower fall-risk groups with 89% accuracy. The system was similarly accurate, between 87 and 92 percent, at identifying specific kinds of balance deficits, such as difficulty reacting quickly or staying steady while walking. Steadiplay produced these results in roughly five to seven minutes, about half the time of the standard clinical exam. Clinicians involved in the study also observed that Steadiplay appeared sensitive to subtle balance differences during tasks with divided attention, which the standard exam did not capture. While this was not formally tested, it points to the platform's potential for catching problems early, when they are most preventable. Participants consistently found the experience enjoyable and motivating, an important quality for any tool meant to encourage repeated practice and improvement.

Broader Impacts: Beyond the research itself, the project worked to raise public awareness about balance health. Steadi Systems participated in four community events across Colorado, reaching more than 200 people of all ages, from intergenerational family programs to older adult research gatherings. Again and again, participants shared that they had noticed changes in their own balance but had not known it was something they could measure or improve. Many left eager to practice, encouraged to learn that balance, like strength, can be trained. The project also brought engineers, physical therapists, and researchers together, and its findings were presented to a regional audience of clinicians at the American Physical Therapy Association meeting in Colorado.

The project further explored how a validated balance tool might reach the people who need it most. Through structured conversations with more than one hundred health care providers nationwide, the team learned that interest in faster, more objective balance assessment spans many settings, including rehabilitation, sports medicine, aging care, and recovery from concussion. Across these settings, providers pointed to the same priorities of low cost, portability, and fast setup, the very qualities Steadiplay was designed around. These conversations confirmed a real-world need and helped guide how the technology can best serve clinics and the patients who depend on them.

Summary: Collectively, the Phase I work showed that a portable, engaging device costing a fraction of the price of high-end clinical balance systems can deliver balance information comparable to expert clinical assessment in less time. The findings also point to a long-standing need in balance research for practical, validated measurement tools that can move fall-risk assessment beyond costly or episodic screening, detect meaningful change over time, and help clinicians decide when early intervention is warranted. By making balance screening faster, more accessible, and more enjoyable, this research lays the groundwork for tools that could help people of all ages protect their mobility, independence, and quality of life while reducing the burden of falls on individuals, families, and the health system.
